analysis.one_liner: Shields generic and biosimilar makers from patent lawsuits over cheaper "skinny label" drugs.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support in January 2025, the bill has received no hearing, no vote, and no floor action in the Senate Judiciary Committee since.
analysis.plain_summary: Generic drugs can be approved for uses no longer protected by a patent through "skinny labeling" — but after a federal court decision, a generic maker could still be sued for patent infringement for marketing a drug that way. This bill writes a safe harbor into law: seeking a skinny label, marketing the drug with it, or telling pharmacists it's equivalent to the brand drug would not count as patent infringement. It applies to both small-molecule generics and biosimilars, and it would even cover lawsuits already in progress.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs whose patents have expired for some uses, since generic makers can stay on the market for the unpatented uses instead of exiting under threat of lawsuits. Also the generic and biosimilar manufacturers themselves, who gain protection from infringement claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients on drugs with expiring patents; generic makers

how_it_helps.text: Skinny labeling lets the FDA approve a generic only for the uses of a drug that are no longer under patent, keeping a lower-cost version available when part of the patent has expired.

A court held in GlaxoSmithKline v. Teva that a generic maker can sometimes be liable for patent infringement just for marketing a skinny-label generic, creating legal risk that can push generics off the market or discourage approval in the first place.

The bill makes it explicit that submitting a skinny-label application, promoting or commercially marketing the drug with that label, and describing it as a generic or therapeutic equivalent of the brand drug are not infringement of a method-of-use patent — so long as the labeling and promotion do not reference the patented uses.
The same safe harbor is extended to biosimilars under the Public Health Service Act, and the bill applies retroactively to conduct and lawsuits pending before enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, whose ability to enforce method-of-use patents against skinny-label competitors through infringement suits — or through the settlement leverage those suits provide — would be curtailed.

drawbacks.text: Brand companies argue that weaker enforcement of method-of-use patents cuts the reward for finding new uses of existing drugs, since a generic could free-ride on the label for a newly approved indication once the patent window narrows.

The safe harbor still does not apply when generic labeling or promotion references the patented conditions of use, so the factual line between protected and infringing marketing would remain a source of litigation rather than eliminating it.
Applying the shield retroactively to lawsuits already in court changes the rules mid-dispute for patent holders who filed in reliance on existing law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for patients is real: keeping generics on the market for out-of-patent uses is one of the cheaper ways to hold drug costs down, and the bill is narrowly aimed at a specific legal vulnerability created by one court decision. The tradeoff is a weaker lever for brand companies to protect investment in new uses of existing drugs, and the carve-out for patented uses keeps some line-drawing disputes alive. On balance the public benefit outweighs those costs, though the bill alone does not address the bigger drivers of U.S. drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in January 2025, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 9, 2025 by Sen. Hickenlooper along with Sens. Welch, Cotton, and Collins.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, and the record shows no further action since.
It has three cosponsors: one Democrat and two Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers keep the current legal leverage over skinny-label generics, since no law has changed; patients and generic makers remain exposed to the infringement risk the bill would have removed.

for.name: Sen. John Hickenlooper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a safe harbor from method-of-use patent infringement for skinny-label generics and biosimilars.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; no action taken
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in January 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — in the time since.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four initial backers span the aisle — one Democrat, one Independent, and two Republicans — though the record shows no committee or floor action for either party to fight over.

industries.note: The bill removes patent-infringement liability for skinny-label products, letting these makers keep cheap versions of drugs on the market. Their gain comes through lower prices for patients, so their interest runs alongside the public's.

The bill curtails their ability to sue skinny-label competitors for method-of-use patent infringement — a tool that also underpins lucrative settlement agreements delaying generic entry. Fewer delayed generics means lower prices for patients.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is still in session, but with a referral to Judiciary and no movement after introduction, the bill faces long odds: most bills at this stage die in committee unless attached to a broader drug-pricing package. Its bipartisan sponsorship gives it a talking point, but nothing more has been scheduled.
